readings.title: The Sky
readings.challenge: Follow a child’s explanation of what she sees, and mark where the explanation goes beyond what she observed.
readings.focus: How a young speaker builds a theory of chains and a puller from a passing shadow and a sky that seems to move.
readings.context: Under the Tree (1922) is Elizabeth Madox Roberts’s book of poems in the voice of a small child growing up in the Kentucky countryside. The poet was a grown woman; the child’s way of seeing is something she made on purpose. A bluejay is a loud blue bird; a poplar is a tall, narrow tree.

excerpt.locator: “The Sky” (p. 1), complete poem; opens “I saw a shadow on the ground And heard a bluejay going by; A shadow went across the…”; closes “…every time I look to see, The sky is always slipping back And getting far away from me.”.

questions.prompt: What does the child see and hear in the first stanza before she looks up?
facilitatorNotes: A shadow crossing the ground and a bluejay going by; only then does she look up. The poem starts with evidence on the ground, which may be why the sky seems to move: something has just passed across it.
evidence: I saw a shadow on the ground
And heard a bluejay going by;

questions.prompt: The sky “hung up on the poplar tree.” What does that tell you about where she is standing and how she judges distance?
facilitatorNotes: From the ground the sky seems to rest on the treetops, as near as the poplar. Her picture of the sky comes from her position, which is why she can believe it later moves away.
evidence: It hung up on the poplar tree,

questions.prompt: What explanation does she offer in the third stanza, and which words show she is guessing?
facilitatorNotes: “I think” and “must be” mark a theory: the sky is tied with chains and pulled from the top. She explains the unfamiliar with something familiar, such as a bucket or gate on a chain. Readers can say what might really be moving: clouds, the bird, or nothing at all.
evidence: I think it must be tied with chains
And something pulls it from the top.

questions.prompt: The sky is “always slipping back / And getting far away from me.” Is this only about the sky, or could it describe a feeling too?
facilitatorNotes: Literally, the sky never comes closer however often she looks. Some readers hear a small disappointment, something wanted that keeps withdrawing; others hear only wonder. Either view should rest on words such as “never,” “always” and “from me.”
evidence: It never has come down again,
The sky is always slipping back

readings.title: On the Hill
readings.challenge: Track how the speaker’s attention moves from the whole town to her own house, and notice what she tries and fails to see.
readings.focus: A view from above makes a familiar place strange, and the child tries to picture herself inside it.
readings.context: Under the Tree (1922) is Elizabeth Madox Roberts’s book of poems in the voice of a small child growing up in the Kentucky countryside. The book’s epigraph quotes two lines of this poem. The courthouse where wagons stop, the public scales for weighing loads and the blacksmith shop mark a small country town of about a century ago.

excerpt.locator: “On the Hill” (p. 24), complete poem; opens “Mother said that we could go Up on the hill where the strawberries grow.”; closes “But Dickie said, "Come on, let's race"; And Will had found the strawberry place.”.

questions.prompt: List the places the child picks out from the hill. In what order does she find them, and where does the list stop?
facilitatorNotes: Playing field, roads, courthouse, bridge, scales, blacksmith shop, church steeple, then her own house under the poplar. The view narrows from the whole town to home, as if she had been searching for it all along.
evidence: And I found the house that we live in.

questions.prompt: Why might the still swing ropes matter more than a swing in motion would?
facilitatorNotes: Nobody is at home to swing; seen from far off, home looks empty without her family. That stillness leads straight into her wish to see “some of us” there.
evidence: The ropes were hanging very still.

questions.prompt: What does she try to see that cannot be seen from the hill that day?
facilitatorNotes: Her house in rain and at lamplight, and her family, herself included, walking under the tree. She is imagining other times and trying to see herself from outside, which no one can quite do.
evidence: Our house when the rain is over it,
And how it looks when I am there.

questions.prompt: Why might the poet end with Dickie’s race and Will’s strawberries?
facilitatorNotes: Other children pull her back from quiet looking into play, and the strawberries return to the reason for the walk in the first lines. Readers may feel the ending as a relief, a small loss, or both.
evidence: But Dickie said, "Come on, let's race";
And Will had found the strawberry place.

readings.title: Father’s Story
readings.challenge: Notice how a young speaker retells a story she has only half taken in.
readings.focus: The poem cares more about the father, the circle of children and the feel of listening than about the story told.
readings.context: Under the Tree (1922) is Elizabeth Madox Roberts’s book of poems in the voice of a small child growing up in the Kentucky countryside. “Dan Tucker” is the popular nineteenth-century comic song “Old Dan Tucker.” Jason, the golden fleece and Troy come from Greek legends.

excerpt.locator: “Father’s Story” (p. 30), complete poem; opens “We put more coal on the big red fire, And while we are waiting for dinner to cook, Our…”; closes “…my place. And I push my fingers into his skin To make little dents in his big rough face.”.

questions.prompt: Who is there, who is missing, and where does each child sit or stand?
facilitatorNotes: Everyone but Clarence. Some sit on Father’s legs, one on the little red chair, and the speaker stands at his arm, “my place.” The fixed places show a family custom repeated many evenings.
evidence: And all of us but Clarence are there.
I stand by his arm, for that is my place.

questions.prompt: How much of the golden fleece story does the child understand? Which words show it?
facilitatorNotes: She calls it “golden wool” and runs Jason, a ship and Troy together, though Troy belongs to a different legend. “Some of it is about” shows she remembers fragments and the sound of names. Readers who know Jason from The Heroes may enjoy catching the mix-up.
evidence: He tells about the golden wool,
And some is about a town called Troy.

questions.prompt: What do the song and the Greek legend have in common in this room, even though they are very different?
facilitatorNotes: Father moves from a comic song to an ancient legend without the children minding; both are simply Father’s performances. The occasion, coal on the fire while dinner cooks, matters as much as the material.
evidence: He sings Dan Tucker Went to Town,
Or he tells us about the golden fleece.

questions.prompt: Why does the poem end with the child making dents in her father’s face instead of with the end of the story?
facilitatorNotes: The last image is touch: closeness to her father outlasts the tale. “Big rough face” gives his size and texture as a small child feels them. Some readers find it tender, some funny; both readings fit.
evidence: To make little dents in his big rough face.

readings.title: Christmas Morning
readings.challenge: Follow an imagined scene built on “if” and “would,” and catch the place where the speaker slips.
readings.focus: A child sets the Nativity on her own farm, and one slip of the tongue shows whose faces she imagines.
readings.context: Under the Tree (1922) is Elizabeth Madox Roberts’s book of poems in the voice of a small child growing up in the Kentucky countryside. In the Christian Gospels, Jesus is born in a stable in Bethlehem and laid in a manger, a feeding trough for animals, and wise men come to visit. The speaker imagines that birth happening in her own family’s barn.

excerpt.locator: “Christmas Morning” (pp. 32–34), complete poem; opens “If Bethlehem were here today, Or this were very long ago, There wouldn't be a winter time…”; closes “…talk would soon begin. And when I'd tiptoe softly out I'd meet the wise men going in.”.

questions.prompt: What does the opening “If” set up? Where does the poem come back to it?
facilitatorNotes: The whole visit is imagined: if Bethlehem were here, or if this were long ago. The fourth stanza ends by repeating the condition with its two halves reversed, a reminder that none of this is happening.
evidence: If Bethlehem were here today,
If this were very long ago

questions.prompt: Which details come from the speaker’s own farm rather than from the Christmas story?
facilitatorNotes: The garden gate, pasture walk and cattle barns, the heavy iron chain and wooden pin, the pigeons and yellow hens. Familiar things let the old story happen in her world.
evidence: I'd move the heavy iron chain
The pigeons and the yellow hens

questions.prompt: Reread “And Mother held my hand and smiled-- / I mean the lady would.” What has the speaker done, and why does she correct herself?
facilitatorNotes: She slips into describing her own mother, in the past tense, as if it had really happened, then corrects herself to “the lady would.” Her Mary seems modeled on her mother, as the baby “would look like our John.” Discuss whether the slip makes the poem feel more real or more personal.
evidence: I mean the lady would
And he would look like our John,

questions.prompt: Why might the poem end as she meets the wise men going in?
facilitatorNotes: She has had a private visit before the story’s famous scene, and hands the stable back to the familiar story as she leaves. Some readers find that modest; others feel she was there first.
evidence: I'd meet the wise men going in.

readings.title: People Going By
readings.challenge: Infer what each passer-by is like from a line or two, and separate what the child knows from what she guesses.
readings.focus: A neighbourhood seen from under a tree: sounds first, then names, habits and rumours.
readings.context: Under the Tree (1922) is Elizabeth Madox Roberts’s book of poems in the voice of a small child growing up in the Kentucky countryside. A rosary is a string of prayer beads used by Catholics. Charming away warts with muttered words was an old country folk practice.

excerpt.locator: “People Going By” (pp. 35–37), complete poem; opens “Before they come I hear their talk And hear their feet go on the walk.”; closes “I can feel them almost speak to me, When they pass by our tree.”.

questions.prompt: How does the child know people are coming before she sees them?
facilitatorNotes: She hears their talk and their feet on the walk. The repeated “some go fast and some go slow” also describes how footsteps sound.
evidence: Before they come I hear their talk
And hear their feet go on the walk.

questions.prompt: Choose one passer-by. What does the child know for certain about that person, and what does she only think or hear said?
facilitatorNotes: Mrs. Warner hurries to the church with the cross; only “I think” tells us she prays there daily. Uncle Mells is lame; the spells are what people say about him. Help readers point to signal words such as “I think,” “maybe” and “almost.”
evidence: I think she goes there every day
He takes off warts by mumbling words,

questions.prompt: What might “far-off looks” suggest about Miss Jane Anne and Mr. Paul?
facilitatorNotes: They walk together at nightfall but hardly talk: perhaps shy, perhaps sad, perhaps simply tired. The child notices without explaining, which leaves room for several readings.
evidence: They go along with far-off looks
And hardly ever talk at all.

questions.prompt: The poem repeats “some of them I almost know” and ends “I can feel them almost speak to me.” What does “almost” say about the child’s place in this neighbourhood?
facilitatorNotes: She knows names and habits but stays outside their lives, watching from under the tree; the passers-by nearly include her. Some readers hear longing, others contentment.
evidence: And some of them I almost know.
I can feel them almost speak to me,

readings.title: The Worm
readings.challenge: Notice how one question changes what the children are doing, and what the poem leaves unanswered.
readings.focus: A digging game turns into wondering about another creature’s mind.
readings.context: Under the Tree (1922) is Elizabeth Madox Roberts’s book of poems in the voice of a small child growing up in the Kentucky countryside. The children are playing at digging wells with a broken spade, a piece of tin and a shell. A clod is a lump of earth.

excerpt.locator: “The Worm” (pp. 50–51), complete poem; opens “Dickie found a broken spade And said he'd dig himself a well; And then Charles took a…”; closes “…in a little wad, And then he stretched himself again And went back home inside the clod.”.

questions.prompt: How do the children treat the worm before Will asks his question?
facilitatorNotes: Dickie makes him wait and stay; the speaker pokes him to watch him squirm. He is something to look at and play with.
evidence: But Dickie made him wait and stay.
I poked him once to see him squirm.

questions.prompt: Which words make the worm’s movements easy to picture?
facilitatorNotes: “Pucker up himself,” “stretch himself,” “puckered in a little wad”; “shining skin was soft and wet.” The verbs treat him as a “himself,” which suits the question that follows.
evidence: We watched him pucker up himself
His shining skin was soft and wet.

questions.prompt: What changes after Will wonders whether the worm knows he is a worm?
facilitatorNotes: They sit back, forget their wells and try to answer. The question stops the game and turns the worm from a plaything into someone who might have a point of view.
evidence: He knows that he's a worm.
And we forgot to dig our wells

questions.prompt: Does the poem answer Will’s question? What does the worm do at the end, and why might the poet stop there?
facilitatorNotes: No answer comes. While they think, the worm goes “back home inside the clod”; calling it home suggests he has his own life whether or not he “knows.” Some readers find it funny that the worm simply leaves the thinkers behind.
evidence: And went back home inside the clod.

readings.title: Water Noises
readings.challenge: Hear how a repeated phrase works like the sound it imitates.
readings.focus: Alone by the stream, the child turns sounds into words and the water into a questioner.
readings.context: Under the Tree (1922) is Elizabeth Madox Roberts’s book of poems in the voice of a small child growing up in the Kentucky countryside. The killdeer is a bird named for its cry; “Killdee” is the child’s way of writing that call.

excerpt.locator: “Water Noises” (pp. 56–57), complete poem; opens “When I am playing by myself, And all the boys are lost around, Then I can hear the water…”; closes “…and have a drink. But when she goes I still can hear The water say, "And do you think?"”.

questions.prompt: When does the child hear the water talk?
facilitatorNotes: Only when she plays by herself and the boys are “lost around,” out of sight. Quiet lets her hear it; readers may compare times they noticed sounds when alone.
evidence: When I am playing by myself,
It makes a little talking sound.

questions.prompt: What does the water seem to say, and how is that different from what the bird says?
facilitatorNotes: The water asks a question that has no end; the bird calls out its own name. The question begins with “And,” as if a conversation had already been going on.
evidence: "And do you think? And do you think?"
"Killdee, killdee!"

questions.prompt: Read the poem aloud. Which words imitate the noises they describe?
facilitatorNotes: “Snaps and ticks,” “ripple up and wink.” “Wink” and “drink” rhyme with “think,” so the water’s question echoes through the poem’s sounds.
evidence: A bug shoots by that snaps and ticks,
I see it ripple up and wink;

questions.prompt: Why does the poem end with the cow leaving and the water still speaking?
facilitatorNotes: Visitors come and go, the bug, the bird, the cow, but the water keeps asking. The question stays with the child, and perhaps it is meant for her, or for the reader, to answer.
evidence: But when she goes I still can hear
The water say, "And do you think?"

readings.title: In the Night
readings.challenge: Decide what is happening in a frightening poem that never says it is a dream.
readings.focus: How the poem makes fear physical and leaves the reader to tell what is real from what is imagined.
readings.context: Under the Tree (1922) is Elizabeth Madox Roberts’s book of poems in the voice of a small child growing up in the Kentucky countryside. The lamp has been turned down low for the night.
readings.contentNote: A child’s night fright: a panther with “bloody bubbles” on its face, and a one-eyed figure whose jaw is “torn away.”

excerpt.locator: “In the Night” (pp. 60–62), complete poem; opens “The light was burning very dim, The little blaze was brown and red, And I waked just in…”; closes “…save myself at all, And so I only waited there And turned my face against the wall.”.

questions.prompt: What clues suggest that the panther and the Something may not be real?
facilitatorNotes: She has only just waked; the light is dim, brown and red; “long marks of light” seem to come from her own eyes, as happens when you are half asleep. Nothing moves toward her. The poem never says “dream,” so readers must judge from such details.
evidence: The light was burning very dim,
Long marks of light came out of my eyes

questions.prompt: How does the poem show fear in the child’s body?
facilitatorNotes: Her throat is shut and dry, her heart jumps, she can neither talk nor cry, and she turns her face to the wall. The fear is shown through her body, never named.
evidence: But all my throat was shut and dry.
My little heart was jumping fast,

questions.prompt: Why might the poet give the Something a capital letter and no name?
facilitatorNotes: It cannot be named, and the capital makes it a strange, important presence. Its stillness, staring without moving or speaking, can be more frightening than an attack.
evidence: Was Something waiting in the room--
But did not move or say a thing.

questions.prompt: In the last stanza, does the child find a way to be safe, or only a way to bear it?
facilitatorNotes: She says she could not save herself, so she waited and turned away. Some readers call her helpless; others say turning away is the one choice left to her. The poem ends without morning or rescue.
evidence: I couldn't save myself at all,
And turned my face against the wall.

readings.title: Shells in Rock
readings.challenge: Connect many separate observations to one idea, then follow the last stanza’s “Suppose.”
readings.focus: A child finds fossil shells everywhere and imagines the sea coming back for them.
readings.context: Under the Tree (1922) is Elizabeth Madox Roberts’s book of poems in the voice of a small child growing up in the Kentucky countryside. Much of Kentucky’s limestone formed on the floor of ancient seas and is full of fossil shells. A quarry is a pit where stone is cut.

excerpt.locator: “Shells in Rock” (pp. 78–79), complete poem; opens “I've been along the quarry road, And I have watched men digging wells, And everywhere it…”; closes “…under all the hills. Suppose the sea should come back here And gather up its shells.”.

questions.prompt: Where has the child seen the shells? What does the length of the list show?
facilitatorNotes: The quarry road, wells, a church, a bridge, foundation stones, creeks, waterfalls, the jail, roads and hills. The shells are everywhere, under the whole landscape and inside its buildings.
evidence: The stones were full of little shells.
And once I saw them on the jail--

questions.prompt: How does the child explain the shells, and where did the explanation come from?
facilitatorNotes: “Some one said” they were left when the ocean went away: a secondhand explanation she accepts. It is close to what geologists say about ancient seas, though she cannot check it herself.
evidence: And some one said that they were left
When the ocean went away.

questions.prompt: Why might the poet put a church, a bridge and a jail in the same list?
facilitatorNotes: The shells take no notice of what people use the stone for; holy, useful and shameful buildings are all made of old sea floor. The point is how ordinary and how widespread the shells are.
evidence: A church, and in a bridge.
More little shells in walls.

questions.prompt: What does the last stanza ask the reader to imagine, and how does it make you feel?
facilitatorNotes: That the sea might return and gather up its shells, taking back the roads and hills built of them. Some find this exciting, others unsettling; the solid ground becomes something on loan from the ocean.
evidence: Suppose the sea should come back here
And gather up its shells.

readings.title: Horse
readings.challenge: Separate what the child sees from what she imagines the horse says.
readings.focus: A silent horse “talks” through the child’s imagination and insists on being himself.
readings.context: Under the Tree (1922) is Elizabeth Madox Roberts’s book of poems in the voice of a small child growing up in the Kentucky countryside. Drab is a dull brownish grey. A bridle is the headgear used to guide a horse; here it hangs on a hitching post.

excerpt.locator: “Horse” (pp. 80–81), complete poem; opens “His bridle hung around the post. The sun and the leaves made spots come down; I looked…”; closes “…as they had been before. He said for me to run along And not to bother him any more.”.

questions.prompt: What does the child see before the horse begins to “talk”?
facilitatorNotes: Spots of sun through leaves, the drab post, the brown horse, his long hard still nose and chalky specks on his lip. She looks closely, through the fence.
evidence: The post was drab and he was brown.
And on his lip were specks like chalk.

questions.prompt: The horse “didn’t talk out with his mouth.” How, then, does he talk?
facilitatorNotes: “The talk was there along his nose; / It seemed and then it was.” She reads his face and stillness and turns them into speech; “it seemed and then it was” traces how an imagined thing becomes real to her.
evidence: The talk was there along his nose;
It seemed and then it was.

questions.prompt: Why does the horse object to being compared with the post?
facilitatorNotes: She had set them side by side as drab and brown; he allows that the colours are nearly the same, but he is not a post to hold a fence. “I’m horse” claims being alive and himself. Readers of Black Beauty may compare another horse who speaks for himself.
evidence: "I'm horse," he said, "that's what!"

questions.prompt: How does the horse end the conversation, and what does that show about him?
facilitatorNotes: He shuts his eyes and tells her to run along: hot, bothered by flies, dignified and a little grumpy. The child imagines a horse with moods of his own and accepts being sent away.
evidence: He said for me to run along
And not to bother him any more.

readings.title: Strange Tree
readings.challenge: Decide how a tree with no face can “look,” and whether the fear comes from the tree or from the child.
readings.focus: On a lonely road a child feels watched by an old bent tree, and the poem never says whether she imagined it.
readings.context: Under the Tree (1922) is Elizabeth Madox Roberts’s book of poems in the voice of a small child growing up in the Kentucky countryside. The Jarboe house is a neighbour’s farmhouse, the last familiar place before the road goes on. Limbs are a tree’s big branches.

excerpt.locator: “Strange Tree” (from p. 46), complete poem; opens “Away beyond the Jarboe house I saw a different kind of tree. Its trunk was old and large…”; closes “…stopped to turn and see, The tree was bending to the side And leaning out to look at me.”.

questions.prompt: Where is the tree, and what does it look like?
facilitatorNotes: “Away beyond the Jarboe house,” past the last house she knows, where the road goes on “to reach some other place.” Its trunk is old, large and bent, with yellow wrinkles. Being past the familiar part of the road matters to how she feels.
evidence: Away beyond the Jarboe house
Its trunk was old and large and bent,

questions.prompt: “I saw a tree that looked at me, / And yet it did not have a face.” How can it look without a face?
facilitatorNotes: It looks “with all its limbs” and “with all its bark”: the whole tree seems to watch her, which is stranger than a pair of eyes would be. Its bent trunk and wrinkles may make it seem like a very old person.
evidence: And yet it did not have a face.
It looked at me with all its limbs;

questions.prompt: What happens when she runs away and turns to look? Could there be an ordinary explanation?
facilitatorNotes: The tree is “bending to the side / And leaning out to look at me.” A grown-up might say a bent tree seen from a new place seems to lean a new way. The poem gives no such explanation; it stays inside the child’s feeling, so the tree seems to follow her.
evidence: And then I ran to get away,
And leaning out to look at me.

questions.prompt: Have you ever felt watched by something that was not alive? Why might the feeling be strongest on a road “going on and on”?
facilitatorNotes: Alone at the edge of the places we know, ordinary things can seem strange. The poem does not laugh at the child for being afraid. Some readers find it eerie; others find it funny; both can point to the last stanza.
evidence: The road was going on and on
And I could feel it look at me.

readings.title: The Hens
readings.challenge: Listen with the child to sounds that are almost words, and decide what the hens might be asking.
readings.focus: At nightfall a child stops in the barn to overhear the hens, and finds a question that nothing answers.
readings.context: Under the Tree (1922) is Elizabeth Madox Roberts’s book of poems in the voice of a small child growing up in the Kentucky countryside. “The Hens” is the last poem in the book. Hens sleep on a perch, a bar high off the ground; pigeons often roosted in church towers. A ruffled sound is the rustle of feathers being shaken out.

excerpt.locator: “The Hens” (from p. 86), complete poem; opens “The night was coming very fast; It reached the gate as I ran past.”; closes “She pushed her head close into her wing, But nothing answered anything.”.

questions.prompt: How does the poem show night coming on?
facilitatorNotes: Night is “coming very fast” and “reached the gate as I ran past,” as if it were racing her home. The pigeons have gone to the church tower and the hens are on their perch. Everything is settling for the night.
evidence: The night was coming very fast;
It reached the gate as I ran past.

questions.prompt: What does the child hear? Why does she call it “A piece of a little purring word”?
facilitatorNotes: A soft murmur, only part of a word, so she cannot be sure of it; “purring” makes it soft and close, like a cat’s sound. She stops and waits to hear more, which shows how much she wants to understand.
evidence: A piece of a little purring word.
To try to hear what the hens were saying.

questions.prompt: She is sure the hens are asking something “over and over again.” What might a hen ask at night?
facilitatorNotes: Readers can invent answers: is everyone home, is it safe, where has the light gone. The poem does not say; the child cannot understand the words, yet “that was plain” to her that it is a question.
evidence: They were asking something, that was plain,
Asking it over and over again.

questions.prompt: “But nothing answered anything.” How does the last line change the feeling of the poem?
facilitatorNotes: The hen tucks her head into her wing and the question just hangs there. Some readers hear loneliness; others hear the peaceful hush of a barn going to sleep. A reader may also think of questions of her own that nobody answers. The plain last words leave room for either feeling.
evidence: She pushed her head close into her wing,
But nothing answered anything.

readings.title: Mumps
readings.challenge: Follow a small family story to its turn, and say what the last stanza shows without being told a lesson.
readings.focus: Dick teases the others about their mumps until he catches them himself, and the teasing stops.
readings.context: Under the Tree (1922) is Elizabeth Madox Roberts’s book of poems in the voice of a small child growing up in the Kentucky countryside. Mumps is an illness that makes the glands in the neck swell; before there was a vaccine nearly every child caught it, and brothers and sisters caught it from each other. Mothers tied up a swollen jaw with a strip of cloth, a “mump rag.” Sour food makes swollen mumps glands ache.

excerpt.locator: “Mumps” (from p. 42), complete poem; opens “I had a feeling in my neck, And on the sides were two big bumps; I couldn't swallow…”; closes “…And cried because his neck was sore, And not a one said sour things To anybody any more.”.

questions.prompt: How does the child know she has mumps?
facilitatorNotes: A feeling in her neck, two big bumps on the sides, and she cannot swallow at all. She describes what she feels, not the name of the illness, until the last word of the stanza.
evidence: And on the sides were two big bumps;
I couldn't swallow anything

questions.prompt: Why does Dick call out “vinegar and lemon drops / And pickles!”?
facilitatorNotes: Even thinking of sour food makes mumps ache, so naming sour things is a way to hurt the others “just to make us cry.” He is the only one without a mump rag, safe for now, and he enjoys it.
evidence: That didn't have a mump rag on.
just to make us cry.

questions.prompt: What happens on Tuesday?
facilitatorNotes: Dick catches mumps, is “very sad,” and cries because his neck is sore. The teaser now feels exactly what he teased the others about.
evidence: But Tuesday Dick was very sad

questions.prompt: “And not a one said sour things / To anybody any more.” What can “sour things” mean here? Is there a lesson, and does the poem say it?
facilitatorNotes: Both the sour foods and unkind words. Now everyone is ill, nobody teases, and the others do not tease Dick back, which is kind. The poem never states a moral; it lets the story show it. Readers can discuss whether Dick deserved some teasing in return.
evidence: And not a one said sour things
To anybody any more.

readings.title: The Circus
readings.challenge: Separate what the child saw from what she guessed and what she only heard someone say.
readings.focus: A circus parade passes through town, and a child’s report mixes wonder, guesses and one thing she refuses to claim she saw.
readings.context: Under the Tree (1922) is Elizabeth Madox Roberts’s book of poems in the voice of a small child growing up in the Kentucky countryside. Travelling circuses paraded through a town’s streets to advertise the show: painted wagons, animals and riders. The Queen of Sheba is a rich queen in the Bible who visits King Solomon. Circuses of the time also showed people as curiosities; a “wild man” was usually a performer dressed up and advertised as a savage from a far country.
readings.contentNote: A man is shown in a cage as a “big wild man,” a cruel and false kind of circus act of the time.

excerpt.locator: “The Circus” (from p. 44), complete poem; opens “Friday came and the circus was there, And Mother said that the twins and I And Charles…”; closes “…going over his feet. And somebody said "He eats them alive!" But I didn't see him eat.”.

questions.prompt: Who goes to see the parade, and what are the first surprises?
facilitatorNotes: She goes with the twins, Charles, Clarence “and all of us.” First come wagons painted with pictures whose doors are shut, so no one can guess what is inside, and a dog with a monkey riding it.
evidence: Could go out and see the parade go by.
And there was a dog that a monkey could ride.

questions.prompt: Find two places where the child guesses rather than knows. What do her guesses show about her?
facilitatorNotes: “You never could guess what they had inside”; “They were queens of Sheba, I guess”; and “a sort of cart,” where she has no name for what she sees. She explains the strange riders with a Bible story she knows, as children do.
evidence: They were queens of Sheba, I guess.
A man on the top of a sort of cart

questions.prompt: “And somebody said ‘He eats them alive!’ / But I didn’t see him eat.” Why does she add the last line?
facilitatorNotes: She reports what someone said but will claim only what she saw herself, which is careful and honest. She may also be a little disappointed, or doubtful about the claim. Readers can say which.
evidence: And somebody said "He eats them alive!"
But I didn't see him eat.

questions.prompt: The “big wild man” is kept in a cage like an animal. How do you feel about that part of the parade? Does the child seem to notice anything wrong?
facilitatorNotes: Circuses advertised people as wild men to thrill crowds; the act was cruel and usually untrue. The child lists him like the elephant, one more sight. Her plain voice lets readers notice what she does not. Some will say a small child could not be expected to see it; others will notice the poem ends on him.
evidence: A big wild man was in a cage,
And he had some snakes going over his feet.

readings.title: In My Pillow
readings.challenge: Work out what the child means by the things she “sees” in her pillow, and why she will not call them dreams.
readings.focus: A child’s private night pictures, blue wings and a talking bowl, are precious to her and slip away as she wakes.
readings.context: Under the Tree (1922) is Elizabeth Madox Roberts’s book of poems in the voice of a small child growing up in the Kentucky countryside. Turning down the light meant lowering the flame of an oil lamp at bedtime.

excerpt.locator: “In My Pillow” (from p. 6), complete poem; opens “When Mother or Father turns down the light, I like to look into my pillow at night.”; closes “And try to feel the pretty things, The little brown bowl and the flying wings.”.

questions.prompt: What does she see in her pillow?
facilitatorNotes: Four birds that are only blue wings, with no heads or feet, flying over a street; and almost every night a little brown bowl that talks to her, laughs and sings. The pictures are strange and exact, as dream pictures often are.
evidence: That were all blue wings and nothing else more.
A little brown bowl that can talk to me,

questions.prompt: “Some people call them dreams, but for me / They are things I look down in my pillow and see.” Why won’t she call them dreams?
facilitatorNotes: To her they are real things in a real place, her pillow; “dreams” is other people’s word for them. She keeps her own name for her own experience. Readers can say what they would call them.
evidence: Some people call them dreams, but for me

questions.prompt: What happens to the pictures when she wakes, and what does she try to do?
facilitatorNotes: They go away “while I am waking,” so she feels her pillow all over, trying to find them as if they were hidden inside it. It is funny and a little sad: she looks with her hands for something that was never there to touch.
evidence: And while I am waking they go away.
I feel my pillow all over and try

questions.prompt: Why does she wait until “nobody is coming by” before she searches?
facilitatorNotes: The pictures are private, and she may expect grown-ups to laugh or tell her they were only dreams. Readers can talk about wonders they keep to themselves, and why.
evidence: And when nobody is coming by,
The little brown bowl and the flying wings.
